title: Verbs, Objects and Complements
summary: Distinguish transitive, intransitive and alternating uses of verbs; recognise when direct objects can be understood but omitted; and choose the prepositional, object-plus-prepositional or object-plus-adjective complements required by particular verbs.
learningObjectives: Recognise verbs that alternate between transitive and intransitive uses when the affected thing becomes the subject, without extending the pattern to unrelated verbs.
Decide when an understood object may be omitted and when a verb requires an explicit object or another complement.
Select obligatory or characteristic verb–preposition patterns, including verbs followed by an object and a prepositional phrase.
Construct object + adjective complements and distinguish their formal style from versions with to be or that-clauses.

explanation.heading: The object can become the subject of a change
explanation.body: Many change-of-state verbs alternate between a transitive use, where an agent acts on something, and an intransitive use, where the affected thing itself is the subject: The caretaker opened the window; The window opened. Break, burn, change, drop, increase and start may work similarly in appropriate senses. This does not license deleting the object from every transitive verb: The designer built a bridge cannot normally become A bridge built in the same sense.
explanation.example: The storm cracked the branch, and later the branch cracked completely.

explanation.heading: Some objects are optional, others are essential
explanation.body: With verbs such as read, eat, cook, sing and drive, an obvious or nonspecific object can sometimes be left unspoken: I have already eaten. Other verbs and individual senses require an object or a further complement. She placed is incomplete if no object and location are supplied; She placed the vase on the shelf supplies both. Do not confuse the ability to omit an understood object with the ability to omit every phrase after a verb.
explanation.example: The musicians played all evening, but the host placed the instruments in storage afterwards.

explanation.heading: Complements can identify place, manner or result
explanation.body: Some verb senses normally need an adverbial or prepositional complement to complete their meaning: The tradition originated in the mountains. Other verbs permit an optional phrase when it adds detail: We paused, or We paused for a moment. Whether a complement is essential depends on the verb and its meaning in context; avoid a universal rule for a verb in every possible use.
explanation.example: The discussion lasted for two hours, then everyone paused briefly.

explanation.heading: Verbs and their required prepositions
explanation.body: Some verbs take a preposition before a complement, such as adhere to, belong to, deal with and specialise in. A separate group takes a direct object followed by a prepositional phrase: associate something with something, attribute a result to a cause, mistake someone for someone else, or put a document on the desk. The preposition is part of the pattern and generally cannot be removed or freely exchanged. The exact form is often determined by the intended meaning.
explanation.example: The research team attributed the improved result to a revised procedure.

explanation.heading: Object + adjective complements and register
explanation.body: Certain verbs can describe an object as having a quality: We considered the timetable unrealistic; They found the office empty. These object + adjective patterns are common with consider, find, judge and declare and may sound formal in some contexts. Depending on the verb, a to be phrase or a that-clause may be more conversational: We considered the timetable to be unrealistic; We considered that the timetable was unrealistic. The adjective describes the object, not the manner in which the action was performed.
explanation.example: The inspector declared the equipment safe after the final check.

comparisons.title: Transitive caused change versus intransitive change

left.label: Agent acts on an object
left.note: Technician is the agent; gap is the direct object.

right.label: Affected subject changes
right.example: The gap widened during the test.
right.note: Gap is now the subject; no direct object appears.

comparisons.title: Adjective as object complement versus adverb modifying a verb

left.label: Object + adjective
left.note: Unsafe describes the corridor that was found.

right.label: Adverbial manner
right.note: Carefully describes how they searched; it is not a quality assigned to the corridor.

examples.sentence: The breeze shut the door, and the door shut without a sound.
examples.note: Shut permits causative and intransitive patterns.

examples.sentence: Lena reads before bed, but her brother reads travel guides.
examples.note: Read may omit an unspecified object or include an explicit one.

examples.sentence: The dispute originated in a minor misunderstanding.
examples.note: The in phrase completes the meaning in this example.

examples.sentence: Please put the labelled samples in the refrigerated cabinet.
examples.note: Put requires a direct object and normally a destination or location complement.

examples.sentence: The committee judged the draft unsuitable for publication.
examples.note: Unsuitable describes the draft as an object complement.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The firm constructed a new station, and a new station constructed last year.
commonMistakes.correct: The firm constructed a new station, and a new station was constructed last year.
commonMistakes.why: Construct does not use the intransitive change-of-state alternation here; the second clause needs a passive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Please put on the laboratory shelf.
commonMistakes.correct: Please put the boxes on the laboratory shelf.
commonMistakes.why: Put needs an object (the boxes) as well as the location phrase in this instruction.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The purple umbrella belongs my neighbour.
commonMistakes.correct: The purple umbrella belongs to my neighbour.
commonMistakes.why: Belong uses to before the person or entity that owns something.
Dangerous is an adjective complement describing the route; dangerously would describe an action.

studyTips: Create transitive–intransitive pairs for break, open and change, then check that both clauses describe the same event from different viewpoints.
Underline every object or complement following a verb; test omission cautiously, especially with place and object + preposition patterns.
Learn verbs in full patterns, such as attribute X to Y and find X adjective, rather than memorising the verb alone.

exercises.prompt: Which pair correctly contrasts a causative transitive use with an intransitive change?
choices: The assistant melted the wax. The wax melted.
The assistant built the stage. The stage built.
The assistant carried the box. The box carried.
exercises.feedback: Melt allows an affected-subject intransitive use, unlike build or carry in these examples.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence omits an understood object in a normal way?
choices: The guide placed carefully.
The driver eats during the break.
The clerk reminded yesterday.
exercises.feedback: Eat can be used without an explicit object when no particular food needs to be named.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct verb + object + preposition pattern.
choices: They attributed the delay for the weather.
They attributed to the weather the delay was long.
They attributed the delay to the weather.
exercises.feedback: Attribute a result to a cause takes a direct object followed by to.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct object + adjective complement after considered.
choices: The assessors considered the evidence reliable.
The assessors considered the evidence reliably.
The assessors considered reliably the evidence.
exercises.feedback: Reliable describes the object evidence, so an adjective is required.

exercises.prompt: The screen ___ when the power returned. Write the past-tense intransitive form of “brighten”.
acceptedAnswers: brightened
exercises.feedback: Brightened is used intransitively when the screen itself becomes brighter.

exercises.prompt: That research group specialises ___ marine biology. Supply the required preposition.
acceptedAnswers: in
exercises.feedback: Specialise in introduces a field of expertise.

exercises.prompt: The committee associated the mistake ___ poor communication. Write the missing preposition.
acceptedAnswers: with
exercises.feedback: Associate something with something else is the required pattern.

exercises.prompt: The judges found the explanation ___ (convince). Write the positive adjective, not an adverb.
acceptedAnswers: convincing
exercises.feedback: Convincing is the adjective complement describing the explanation.

exercises.prompt: Correct the transitive-only mistake: The engineer designed the bridge and the bridge designed quickly.
acceptedAnswers: The engineer designed the bridge and the bridge was designed quickly.
exercises.feedback: Design does not permit the intransitive affected-subject pattern here; use passive was designed.

exercises.prompt: Correct the incomplete put construction by adding the object “the folder”: She put on the cabinet.
acceptedAnswers: She put the folder on the cabinet.
exercises.feedback: Put needs a direct object, here the folder, as well as the location on the cabinet.

exercises.prompt: Correct the preposition: The discovery was attributed with a new detection method.
acceptedAnswers: The discovery was attributed to a new detection method.
exercises.feedback: Attribute something to a cause; passive is attributed to, not attributed with.

exercises.prompt: Correct the adjective complement: The reviewers found the proposal impractically.
acceptedAnswers: The reviewers found the proposal impractical.
exercises.feedback: The adjective impractical describes the proposal; the adverb impractically is unsuitable here.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the intransitive counterpart to “The wind opened the gate.” Retain the gate as subject and use simple past.
acceptedAnswers: The gate opened.
speakingExercises.feedback: Open can describe the affected gate as subject without an object.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say a two-sentence pair in this order using exactly the facts: The cook / burn / the toast. Then: The toast / burn. Use simple past.
acceptedAnswers: The cook burned the toast. The toast burned.
The cook burnt the toast. The toast burnt.
speakingExercises.feedback: Both the transitive and intransitive patterns are possible with burn; burnt and burned are accepted regional variants.

speakingExercises.prompt: State a routine without naming the object. Facts: Mina / read / every evening. Use present simple.
acceptedAnswers: Mina reads every evening.
speakingExercises.feedback: Read can omit an unspecified object in this context.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give a full instruction with verb, object and destination. Facts: Put / the sealed envelope / in the drawer.
acceptedAnswers: Put the sealed envelope in the drawer.
speakingExercises.feedback: Put requires the object and its destination here.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use the fixed verb–preposition pattern. Facts: These keys / belong / to / the caretaker. Use present simple.
acceptedAnswers: These keys belong to the caretaker.
speakingExercises.feedback: Belong to specifies the owner or person responsible.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use object + prepositional phrase. Facts: They / attributed / the cancellation / to / the storm.
acceptedAnswers: They attributed the cancellation to the storm.
speakingExercises.feedback: Attribute X to Y names the event and its alleged cause.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce an object + adjective sentence. Facts: We / found / the instructions / confusing.
acceptedAnswers: We found the instructions confusing.
speakingExercises.feedback: Confusing is an adjective describing the instructions, not the finding action.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say two complete sentences in this order. First: The analyst / considered / the figures / inaccurate. Second: The analyst / considered / the figures / to be / inaccurate.
acceptedAnswers: The analyst considered the figures inaccurate. The analyst considered the figures to be inaccurate.
speakingExercises.feedback: Both patterns attribute the quality inaccurate to figures; to be makes the complement explicit.

listeningExercises.audioText: During the cold night the water froze, and by morning the pipes had cracked.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which change is described without an agent or direct object?
choices: Someone cracked the pipes with a tool.
The water and pipes changed state themselves.
The pipes were transported to the basement.
listeningExercises.feedback: Froze and had cracked are intransitive changes affecting the subjects.

listeningExercises.audioText: I cook most evenings, but on Fridays my brother prepares dinner.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the first clause show about cook?
choices: It may appear without an explicit object.
It always requires the object dinner.
It must be followed by a location.
listeningExercises.feedback: I cook is complete even though the food is not named.

listeningExercises.audioText: The antiques belonged to a small local museum.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the two-word verb phrase before “a small local museum”.
acceptedAnswers: belonged to
listeningExercises.feedback: Belonged to includes the preposition required by the verb.

listeningExercises.audioText: The researchers attributed the improvement to a revised testing method.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which relationship does the sentence express?
choices: The improvement was unrelated to testing.
The method was stored in a cabinet.
The revised method was identified as a cause of the improvement.
listeningExercises.feedback: Attribute X to Y assigns the reported cause Y to outcome X.

listeningExercises.audioText: The supervisor put the emergency kit beside the exit before the visitors arrived.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does beside the exit contribute to the sentence?
choices: It describes how suddenly the kit was put down.
It supplies the location of the kit.
It renames the supervisor.
listeningExercises.feedback: Put takes an object, the emergency kit, and a location complement, beside the exit.

listeningExercises.audioText: The panel considered the proposed timetable unrealistic.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the role of unrealistic?
choices: An adjective describing the timetable.
An adverb describing how the panel considered it.
The object of a preposition.
listeningExercises.feedback: Unrealistic is an object complement assigned to the timetable.

listeningExercises.audioText: The engineer associated the fault with a loose connector.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the four-word prepositional phrase immediately after “fault”.
acceptedAnswers: with a loose connector
listeningExercises.feedback: With a loose connector is the prepositional phrase after associated the fault.

listeningExercises.audioText: The manager found the new arrangement efficient.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the one-word adjective at the end of the sentence.
acceptedAnswers: efficient
listeningExercises.feedback: Efficient is the object complement describing the arrangement.
